Press Release:


Dewani trial : 3
Startling revelations from Anni Dewani’s closest confidant, cousin Sneha Mashru, dominated proceedings in week three of the Shrien Dewani trial. Evidence of shoddy investigation surfaced when the defence lambasted a ballistics expert for substandard work. Carte Blanche unpacks the latest from the trial.


Script:


DEWANI WEEK 3 FINAL MIX

John Webb: The Shrien Dewani trial in Cape Town, as with all high-profile cases, is attracting local and international media--- with photographers vying for position in their quest for the money shots.

Sometimes they get lucky, like when earlier this week, the car carrying State witness and Anni’s cousin, Sneha Mashru, got caught up at an intersection.

Despite the fact that the trial has entered its third week, there is still massive media interest in the arrival to Court each day of Shrien Dewani, as well as members of both families, witnesses, and the two sets of legal counsel.

It doesn’t matter how many times a photographer has taken a picture of a family member or witness, for example, they’ll continue snapping away. It’s in their DNA.

Present throughout this trial has been award-winning photographer Fanie Jason, who has been described as South Africa’s only true paparazzo.

He was the very first photographer to arrive at the crime scene when Anni was murdered.

Fanie Jason: “I was shooting from over a wall. Eventually I got onto the roofs of the houses in Khayelitsha, trying to look at who’s lying in the car.”

John Webb: If he’s not busy taking pictures or trying to glean information from relevant parties, he’s inside court listening to evidence.

Like other journalists covering the case, he is especially interested in how evidence is unfolding, which may suggest that the person sentenced for shooting Anni was not the triggerman.

Fanie Jason: “Because Xolile Mgeni was saying that he was adamant that he didn’t shoot her, he said ‘Yes I was on the crime scene, but I didn’t shoot—I was not the shooter.’”

John Webb: Especially since gunpowder residue was found on the gloves of Mziwamadoda Qwabe, who struck a plea bargain with the State and said that Xolile Mgeni was in fact the shooter.

Sound: “You are sentenced to life imprisonment.”

John Webb: And in a dramatic week, further evidence was led to fuel the perception that the previous Court may have got it wrong after being misled by a crucial State witness.

Day 6 started with evidence of British journalist, Nick Parker.

When Nick Parker, The Sun journalist, took the stand, he gave details about an interview that he conducted with Shrien Dewani about a week after the shooting. Significantly, he said that in that interview, there was no mention made of a surprise helicopter trip.

Yet it was in Dewani’s plea explanation, which was handed up to Court on Day 1 of the trial. The State alleges that he paid R15000 to the hit man to kill Anni. Dewani says that the money was given to taxi driver, Zola Tongo, to organize a surprise helicopter trip for his new wife.

Francois Marais: “Most of the time our bookings are made from our travel partners, from inbound tour operators, travel agencies, and hotel tourist desks.”

John Webb: Although not linked to the case, we asked Francois Marais, a seasoned pilot based at the Waterfront in Cape Town, if ever taxi drivers made bookings for their clients.

Francois Marais: “I’ve never seen a taxi driver arriving here with a bag full of money and saying I’m booking passengers, and here they are.”

John Webb: We asked Defense Attorney William Booth just how significant it was that Dewani did not mention the helicopter trip in his interview with Gerald Parker.

William Booth: “It can’t just be pushed aside and said well look, you know, don’t place any reliance on it, but I don’t think one should get too excited about it. I don’t think one should say because of that one factor, the State has now suddenly latched on to something that they’re going to be able to prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt.”

John Webb: Booth believes that the State’s case rests on forensic evidence, as well as the testimony of the man who had struck plea bargains with the State.

William Booth: “So those are important witnesses and if their evidence falls short and they’re not credible, well then it really doesn’t matter if there’s this version about the helicopter payment.

John Webb: Next up for the State was Anni’s cousin.

Day 6 of the trial dominated by the evidence and cross-examination of Sneha Mashru, Anni’s closest confidant and her cousin. She said that in the days and weeks that followed the shooting, she became increasingly suspicious of Shrien Dewani’s behavior.

So much so that she reported her suspicion to the British police. She said that she and Anni were so close, they even shared the same email passwords. She confirmed an SMS sent to her by Anni, who wrote, ‘What should I do? It is past one day and I feel as I did before. Really trying… he’s a really good guy in all ways but I don’t feel happy with him at all.’

She also added that Anni told her before coming to South Africa that she was thinking of getting a divorce. Advocate Van Zyl objected to this hearsay evidence. Judge Traverso agreed and said, ‘I’m not going to allow an atmosphere to be created in this Court by inadmissible evidence.’

Sneha Mashru went on to say that Dewani’s behavior was puzzling after the death of Anni. She referred to when he tried to force bangles onto her swollen arms, as she lay in a funeral parlor. She said, ‘I could not see the love. He did not look to me as someone who is grieving.’

How much attention do you think the judge will pay to that?

William Booth: “Well again, it’s only a perception, and she’s certainly not an expert that can come to Court and tell the Court, ‘Look because someone has reacted in a certain way, you can draw inferences from that’ You know, people react in all sorts of ways. You know, someone who has just heard of the death of a relative or a loved one might burst into tears, run around crazy; others might just go into complete shock, say nothing, and behave as if they are quite normal.”

John Webb: On Day 7, Sergeant Cornelius Mellett took the stand. He was at the Harare police station when Dewani walked in after the hijacking. He said that his appearance was clean and did not look like a person who had been involved in a struggle. Under cross-examination, he said that Dewani had cried in the police station. He told the Court that when he drove Dewani back to his hotel, he felt that he did not seem as worried as he thought he should be.

Day 8 belonged to the Defense.

One of the biggest talking points of Week 3 was the torrid cross-examination endured by police ballistics expert, warrant officer Peter Engelbrecht.

Peter Engelbrecht, a ballistics expert, was grilled about his evidence at the Mgeni trial. Qwabe had said that Mgeni was sitting in the front left seat and was the shooter. When the Court asked Engelbrecht if he believed that the person who shot Anni was in the front left seat, he said yes. He admitted this week to taking no measurements to support his theory.

The Defense weighed in. ‘How were you able as an expert witness to give that opinion evidence under oath, when on your own version, you didn’t have any basis for saying so?’

He responded that he must have misunderstood the question from the Court.

Then the Defense said, ‘Would you agree with me that your answer very clearly could have misled the Court about your opinion?’ To which the witness replied, ‘Ja, Edele.’

He then went on to say that only recently had he taken measurements of the car; not the crime scene car, but a different model.

The Defense pointed out that all the configurations were wrong- different seats and positioning. The Judge addressed him: ‘It seems that the measurements are of utmost importance in coming to a conclusion and those measurements must be exact, am I wrong?’ Engelbrecht said, no, she was right.

David Klatsow: “All of these things should be done as close to the time of the commission of the crime as possible while you’re investigating it. To come along later with all the measurements and to make the measurements in such a way that they turn out to be inaccurate is not a good idea.”

John Webb: For David Klatsow, inaccurate forensics are unforgivable.

David Klatsow: “It would be what you would call in legal terms, manna from heaven, because it gives the Defense an ideal opportunity to expand on that. It’s the thin end of the cross-examination wedge, and you can do so much damage to the expert or to the police personnel on the other side, that it renders their testimony largely nugatory.”

John Webb: William Booth believes that the concessions made by Engelbrecht could have led to an appeal in the Mgeni case.

William Booth: “Mgeni has passed away, but that is a factor that could have been, you know, latched on to by Mgeni’s lawyers, and said, well, ‘Hang on, you know, a lot of evidence is coming out which is new evidence. We may have considered approaching the Court for an appeal.’ But look he’s dead, so that is pretty academic.

John Webb: So how does Williams Booth see the trial unfolding so far?

William Booth: “Well, Qwabe has not stood well under cross-examination, we’ve had the issue of the sexuality being excluded by the Judge, and then recently we’ve had the criticism of the forensic ballistic expert, Engelbrecht, so I don’t think it’s going particularly well for the State.”

John Webb: Nor does it appear to have gone well for Engelbrecht, who is still under oath and back in the stand tomorrow.
